title: my job hunt - job input list for `python3 -m jobhunt add --json <file>`
description: A JSON array of jobs. One object per job. Only `source` and `title` are required; every other field may be omitted or null. Unknown fields are rejected so a typo cannot be silently ignored. This schema is validated by the app itself (hand-rolled check of the subset of keywords used here: type, enum, required, additionalProperties, properties, items, minLength, pattern).

source.description: Where the job came from. Decides which source_job_id patterns are recognised and which field the board shows as origin.

source_job_id.description: The site's own job id, as a string. If omitted, the app extracts it from `url`: linkedin `jobs/view/<id>` or `jobPosting/<id>`, jobsdb `job/<id>`, greenhouse `/jobs/<id>`. Keep leading zeros and any non-numeric suffix exactly as the site shows them.

url.description: The public job page. Tracking parameters (utm_*, trk, refId, trackingId, e, lipi) are stripped when the canonical URL is computed, so the same job arriving with different tracking still dedupes.

company.description: Hiring company as shown in the posting or email. Null when unknown.

title.description: Job title as shown. Required: it is what the pre-filter matches and what the board shows.

location.description: Free text, e.g. "Bangkok, Thailand" or "Singapore". Used by the location gate through the facts extracted from the JD, not parsed here.

posted_at.description: Posting or email date. Date only (YYYY-MM-DD) or full ISO 8601 with offset. A bare date is read as Asia/Bangkok midnight. Used only by the `posted_within_days` pre-filter.

jd_text.description: Full job description text as plain text. Truncated to 6000 characters before it goes to the model; the full text stays in the store.

email_snippet.description: The alert-email snippet, when there is no JD. The job is flagged jd_missing and scored from this.

salary_text.description: Salary exactly as written in the posting, e.g. "THB 35,000-45,000 per month". Free text; the model extracts the numbers, Python scores them.
